description:
We are Health Signal, a team of two from Switzerland at the Lucerne local event: space enthusiasts who love to explore ideas outside our own domain.

Tamas Kaljuste: business development executive in digital transformation and an AI practitioner focused on practical applications and rapid prototyping. He leads the architecture, the data choices and the build with AI agents.

Sven: young student and co-designer, with the unexpected questions and bold ideas that move the project forward. He decides what looks right and whether an explanation makes sense to a young astronaut.

Our mission: bring the astronauts back from Mars alive, in as good health as possible. Our vision: share what we learn to improve life on Earth.
summary:
On a Mars mission, a question to the doctor on Earth and its answer take up to 43 minutes, and for about 12 days there is no link at all. The crew must judge their own health and act on it. Health Signal is health monitoring that works without waiting for Earth.

Two working apps run on one simulated 999-day Mars mission build on real data. The Habitat App gives each astronaut a daily picture: a body figure, a readiness score and every value against their own normal and the limits of NASA's crew health standard, with what to do next. The Arm Unit on the suit's forearm follows a Mars walk second by second and says Go, Caution or Return on the spot. In both, the astronaut simply asks an AI assistant, by voice, and hears the answer. The rules decide; the AI only explains.

It is data-driven: the mission is simulated from 20 real datasets, among them Curiosity's radiation and weather records, the Inspiration4 crew's blood values and NASA's human health risks, and every value is labelled. Built for Mars, the same approach could help people on Earth who are far from a doctor.
details:
Our mission: bring the astronauts back from Mars alive, in as good health as possible.

What Health Signal is

Health monitoring software for a Mars crew that cannot wait for Earth. It watches body and environment around the clock, warns on the spot with built-in limits, and answers the moment an astronaut asks. Fixed rules, plain code and not AI, raise every warning. Two working apps share one simulated mission:

  • Habitat App, the daily view. A body figure with twelve regions, a readiness score from 0 to 100 and charts over time. Every value is shown against the astronaut's own normal and against its limit, with why it matters and what to do. Earth's instruction arrives once a day, after the signal delay.
  • Arm Unit, the suit's forearm screen. During a Mars walk it reads body, suit and radiation every second and shows one word (Go, Caution, Return), how long the astronaut can stay and the next step. Four complete walks can be played, one of them in a solar storm.
  • The assistant, in both apps. Real-time voice to voice: press the microphone, ask ("Can I go outside tomorrow?") and hear the answer in a few plain sentences. Typing works too. It is given only the values of that moment, the rule results and Earth's instruction, and it never raises or clears a warning.

The Habitat App on mission day 356 (simulated data):

The Arm Unit during a Mars walk (simulated data):

Try it

  • Website and both apps, no login: healthsignal.space · Habitat App · Arm Unit
  • User manuals (PDF): Habitat App · Arm Unit
  • Source code, the simulated database and the documentation (Apache-2.0): github.com/kaljuste/health-signal
  • The website is also the evidence. Its tabs open up the plan, the foundations, the data and the technical detail behind the apps: How it works, Mission, Risks, Measures, Data, Simulation and Database, where every table of the mission can be searched and downloaded.
  • Every screen works without a key, and the rules answer in text. Live AI answers and the voice need a key (initially works without key for limited time); the manuals explain how to use your own limited one.

Why a simulation, and why it is a framework

Nobody has flown to Mars, so no health data from such a mission exists. Instead of inventing numbers, we built one complete mission from real measurements: 999 days, four fictional astronauts, 76 values, 212,789 records with about 1.9 million measured values, and four Mars walks second by second. A fixed seed makes it reproducible.

Three things work today, and each can be improved on its own. The data: add a new dataset or research result and generate the mission again. The apps: they read one database, so real sensors and an astronaut's own measurements need only a connector that writes into the same tables (not built yet). The advisor: a stronger AI model or a larger knowledge base.

The data behind it

We examined 57 sources and kept the 20 datasets that could teach the simulation something:

  • Radiation and solar storms: Curiosity's RAD detector on Mars and LRO CRaTER in deep space, replayed from the matching phase of the last solar cycle; storm timing from NASA DONKI, the OMNI proton record and NOAA's event list. Mission total: 792 mSv; NASA's career limit of 600 mSv is passed on day 786.
  • Mars and the cabin: Curiosity REMS weather at Gale crater; cabin temperature, humidity and CO₂ recorded on the International Space Station (NASA OSDR).
  • The body: blood values of the Inspiration4 crew (NASA OSDR, OSD-569 and OSD-575) and NHANES for healthy baselines; open studies of exercise, sleep loss and head-down tilt for how heart rate, lactate, reaction time and heart rate variability behave. The four crew members are fictional.
  • Limits and risks: NASA-STD-3001 and NASA's medical technical briefs for every limit; the Human Research Program's 22 health risks, each linked to the values we watch; NASA's ranking of medical conditions for how likely events are.
  • The mission plan: computed with JPL Horizons: launch 3 Sep 2037, landing at Gale crater 22 Feb 2038, departure 6 Sep 2039, home 14 Mar 2040, with the signal delay and the 12-day blackout.

Every value carries a label that says how it was made: REAL, REPLAY (real history replayed onto 2037), MODEL (an estimate), SIM (simulated) or COMPUTED. The Data and Simulation tabs of the website show each dataset, why we chose it, what we took from it, and how the result compares with real crews.

Technology

  • Website and apps: HTML, CSS and JavaScript without a framework; the pages read the mission's SQLite database directly in the browser (sql.js).
  • Data and simulation: Python 3 (standard library) for the data pipeline, the mission planner and the reproducible generator; SQLite.
  • Real-time voice to voice with an AI model: speech recognition (the browser's own, or ElevenLabs speech to text), a language model (Anthropic Claude Haiku 5.5 through OpenRouter) that streams its answer, and the ElevenLabs v4 voice, speaking sentence by sentence while the answer is still being written. AI chat by typing uses the same path.
  • Around it: a small Python server that keeps all keys away from the browser; our own design system with three open fonts; a German version; a live view that lets an audience follow the Arm Unit on their phones; Docker containers behind a Cloudflare Tunnel.
  • Film: AI-generated (Google Veo, ElevenLabs).

How we built it: human-led, agent-accelerated

Health Signal shows what a very small team can do when people lead and AI agents accelerate: real data and space-medicine science, brought into a working product at a pace that was not possible before. We set the goal, the story and the architecture, chose which data to trust, directed the look, reviewed and tested the results and took the decisions. AI agents, working in parallel under that direction, did the heavy lifting.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI), in full:

  • Research and data: agents (Claude Code, Anthropic's Claude models) searched and read NASA documents and datasets and wrote the tools that fetch them. We selected the 20 datasets; every limit traces to its source document.
  • Simulation: agents wrote the generator's code from our specification. Its numbers are computed from the real datasets and stated models, not produced by a language model. The written analyses of key days and the knowledge notes were drafted with AI and reviewed by us.
  • Software: agents wrote the code of the website, both apps and the server. We reviewed, ran and corrected it, with a human in the loop and automated browser tests.
  • Text and design: documentation, manuals and these texts were drafted with AI and edited by us; colours, icons and the logo mark were made as code with AI under our direction.
  • Inside the product and the film: the assistant is an AI language model with a synthetic voice (no real person's); it only explains. The film is AI-generated.

The idea, the story, the architecture and the framework concept are ours. We did not choose from AI-made options: we architected the solution ourselves and worked iteratively, challenging and improving what the AI suggested. AI was our builder first of all, and also a supporting expert and a critic of our own work. No NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers appear in any generated content.

Impact and what is new

The crew acts on a warning in seconds instead of waiting 43 minutes. We turned the delay into the design: the rules act on the spot, and Earth's advice becomes a conversation. The whole mission plays like a film, any day and any second of a Mars walk. Our vision: share what we learn to improve life on Earth, where many people also live with plenty of health data and no expert at hand: crews on polar stations and ships, people living alone, patients between doctor visits. That is a vision, not what we built.

Honest limits

Not a medical device. The data is simulated, built from real data. The assistant can be wrong, which is why it never decides. In this demonstration the AI model and the voice are cloud services; on a real mission they would run on board.
